Gas-Powered Chainsaw, released in SABBAT, not V:TES or Jyhad,
shouldn't be a melee weapon either. No matter how hard you hit
someone with a chainsaw, it's the chain rotating that does the damage,
so it shouldn't benefit from any strenght bonuses. As James Coupe
said, neither Talbot's nor the original Chainsaw were listed as melee
weapons - and probably for good reason.

there's no good reason to alter what the card says, then it shouldn't
be changed. Even though Gas-Powered Chainsaw ought to be a non-melee
weapon, it doesn't significantly affect the game that someone can play
Torn Signpost and strike with it for 5 -- so nothing gets changed.

Messages.Body:
On Sun, 3 Sep 2000, Derek Ray wrote:

> On Sun, 03 Sep 2000 01:22:43 GMT, akais...@my-deja.com wrote:

> >Talbot's is not ?
>
> Gas-Powered Chainsaw, released in SABBAT, not V:TES or Jyhad,
> shouldn't be a melee weapon either. No matter how hard you hit
> someone with a chainsaw, it's the chain rotating that does the damage,
> so it shouldn't benefit from any strenght bonuses. As James Coupe
> said, neither Talbot's nor the original Chainsaw were listed as melee
> weapons - and probably for good reason.

I agree that the original 2 are not melee weapons, and were printed that
way intentionally, and should stay that way 'cause "fixing" them is not
worth the confusion and extra errata. However, I think that the
designation of "melee weapon" on "gas powered chainsaw" is a good thing,
and, in retrospect, probably would have been a good thing on Chainsaw &
Talbots as well (both being rather underpowered).

The fact that all the chainsaws (including "gas powered") are not based on
hand damage (unlike almost all other melee weapons since the V:tES
revisions) limits them very much. Thus, you cannot use any chainsaw in
combo with Fists of Death, or Torn Signpost, or inherent hand damage
bonuses, or Ritual Challenge, or Depravity. Sure, with Gas-Powered you
can manage a "Lucky Blow" or with Potence you could play Undead Strength
and potentially boost it indefinitely with Increased Strength, but your
options are far more limited than with Hand-Damage-based weapons.

A chainsaw is a very heavy weapon, and it depends on some pressure as well
as its rotation. It would be odd, I think, to argue that strength is
COMPLETELY irrelevant to its effective use in hand to hand
combat. Strength is merely LESS relevant than it would be for a bastard
sword. Such a situation is simulated by having both weapons designated as
"melee", but only the bastard sword based on hand-damage.

In the original Jyhad set, Bastard Swords and similar melee weapons were
not based on hand-damage, and could only benefit from those strength
bonuses that effected melee weapons. Therefore, the designers decided
that Chainsaws were not melee weapons at all, in order to simulate the
lesser effect of strength. Then the V:tES set further boosted melee
weapons by basing them on hand damage, leaving the poor chainsaws far
behind. The Sabbat set finally allowed the GP chainsaw to catch up a
little bit by designating it a "melee weapon" but not basing it on hand
damage.

> "The card says so" is the very basis of any CCG, by the way. If
> there's no good reason to alter what the card says, then it shouldn't
> be changed. Even though Gas-Powered Chainsaw ought to be a non-melee
> weapon, it doesn't significantly affect the game that someone can play
> Torn Signpost and strike with it for 5 -- so nothing gets changed.

Well, actually you CAN'T do that, because Torn Signpost do not boost melee
weapons unless they are based on hand damage. Other things that you
cannot do are strike more than once in a combat (apparently the things run
out of gas REAL fast). Compare a bastard sword (which costs the same).
You can continue to strike with it on subsequent rounds, and it benefits
from multiple strikes as well. The Gas-Powered Chainsaw needed to be a
melee weapon, if only so it would not COMPLETELY suck in comparison with a
bastard sword. As it is, the GCP is better only if you are certain you
will not have any hand damage, additional strikes, or additional rounds of
combat.

Incidentally, Talbots chainsaw DOES benefit from multiple strike per
round, which might seem odd for a chainsaw. But it is hard to complain of
lack of realism when dealing with an obviously supernatural artifact.

-- John Whelan

Well, overpowered with limitations, if that makes any sense. Once you

this problem, you are in possession of one of the nastiest weapons in
the game - and it comes with a built-in Rush.

>and would cite a noted Jyhad player who declared that, when it was in

>
>>you are on a slow spiral to

Well, you ARE. The 30-Arms Dealer deck, for example, will eventually
run out of Arms Dealers to apply the damage to. I have a version that
uses multiple Restorations to drop blood back into the vampires, and
eventually I will run out of Restorations. I have another version
that uses Embraced Tremere and the Chantry (the "yo-yo" method), but
eventually either you'll run out of blood, pool, or Embraces (when
people get tired of watching you bounce, and intercept their hunt).
But just because you're on the way down doesn't mean you can't make
sure everyone else goes with you, and then you come back up (by
eventually killing the bearer of Talbot's with its own damage). =)

The only deck that avoids this is the Ambrosius deck, and that
requires an awful lot of Ambrosius to make sure you get him BEFORE you
get the Chainsaw. Off the top of my head, I'm not sure there's any
way to fish through your library and locate a retainer, so it really
depends entirely on luck of the draw.

Yes but my in my playgroup we play with new decks almost everytime we
meet up. So it's totally impossible to predict what the others will
play and thus make a counterstrategy for a 20 Governs deck for example.
We also allow repeated actions since we have a CL. There cna be tons of
arguments for and against, but I think every playgroup should be
allowed to play as they think is the best. Nobody in our playgroup has
ever wanted a change and there's another playgroup in the city next to
ours that also play by the same houserules as we do. That totals about
25 people. We're all happy about how it's now. I think a great benefit
with CL is that you know how many cards you need to collect as well.
For example there's no point in getting more than 4 of a rare, so if
someone gets a 5th he'll trade it away, which allows the newbies to get
a chance to trade for some nice cards. And I think it feels just
generally good to have a limit as to how many cards you need to
collect, or worry about getitng played. The major point is that anyone
can win with a deck based on only a few cards, I think it's a quite
lame tactic to be frank. It doesn't require much of skill and makes the
game really boring for the others. As I said, since people change their
decks constantly here you cannot really counter it either, because if
you try to and he's changed thedeck, your own deck might not be all
that good anymore.

And I think also that you should make a deck as you feel like playing
it, and not contruct one only because "you have to counter someone
else's", how fun is that?

There's arguments that with a CL you can still get around it by using 4
Rampage and 4 Arson for example, that has the same effect. Well while
this is true, they're not exactly the same, Rampage requires potence
for example, and if you try go Earth Meld and Majesty combo it's the
same thign. It DOES affect your deck negatively to have to throw in a
lot of skill cards ot make the combo work etc. Most importantly
however, is that of the truly great cards, there's no similar cards
(like immortal grapple) so for these you can only have 4. Same goes
with Temptation of Greater Power etc etc. But as I said, every
playgroup should go for what they feel is thebest. This is what we feel
is the best solution for us.

My 2 cents,
cantila

not allowed to have enough of those counters. You're not allowed all
your S:CE counters because you can't have enough IG. You're not allowed
enough vote counters, because you can't have enough Delaying Tactics.
You're not allowed enough bleed bounces, because you can only have 8 in
Dominate and only 4 in Auspex. Auspex, under NCL, has a very good bleed
defence. You're not allowed good defence against the Brujah lot,
because you can't have enough Leather Jackets and Fake Outs.

>Sure eveyone can try make a deck that specifically deal with the LoP
>deck,

vote deck.

Building a specific counter deck is a pointless exercise. You need a
good amount of defence against a deck, along with a decent deck as well.

defend against combat. If you don't, you'll be dead, CL or no CL.

It's an interesting challenge, and one that has been beaten. Playing
Direct Intervention, Delaying Tactics, Surprise Influence etc., gives
you a good chance against many vote decks. Vote lock isn't solely
generated via Legacy of Pander, you know?

If you go into a game with no vote defence, it doesn't matter if it's 10
Legacy of Pander. You could go and face 1 of each Praxis Seizure in the
game, instead, and you'd still be screwed. Would the variety of Praxis
Seizures make the game any more "fun"?

>It would be so boring for everyone except maybe the
>player himself unless you knew he was going to make such a deck and
>then could prepare yourself (but as I said, we constantly make new
>decks).

If a deck has no way to defend itself against politics, it will die when
it sits next to politics. If a deck has no way to defend itself against
bleed, it will die when it sits next to bleed. If a deck has no way to
defend itself against combat, it will die when it sits next to combat.

These are facts.

You should consider what defences your deck has when you build it.

So, you know you're not going to sit next to 10 Legacy of Pander. Do
you put no vote defence in? Vote lock can be achieved via other means.

If you need to "prepare yourself" against a specific deck, you are
playing badly - and the reason you need xCL to balance decks is because
you're playing badly, not because NL is broken. It sounds like you're
not putting *any* vote defence in at all. LoP can be badly screwed by
generic vote defence, and if you don't put any of that in, well, that's
your own fault, not the fault of NL or LoP. Or another vote deck.

>cards of all our 25 players, and I don't have more than 4 of any rare

can't play an effective politics deck - which he could if you'd let him
put more than 4 Bewitching Orations in. But, for some reason, you
decide to punish him for not being rich, where NL said "Yep, we're cool

rare".

in them do very well indeed. If you *want* to play a deck with mostly
rares, you can do that too - but a common deck won't fall down just
because it's common. It'll fall down because it's badly made.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 6 Sep 2000 23:20:53 +0100, James Coupe wrote:

>Look harder - and whilst you're doing that, look at some of the NL/CL
>debates that have gone before (try Judith and Mark's Jyhad Page, search
>for it) so you don't just repeat the same tired old arguments that have
>been refuted a hundred times before.

You're the one with the same tired old refrain that you repeat again
and again. Trying to silence the argument in this way clearly doesn't
work. I've read the old argmuments in favour of NCL and, while I
understand them, I'm not overly impressed by them.

And there are some new facts to take into account now that the game is
being relaunched. Telling people to go and buy cheap boxes of Jyhad
to get the large multiples they need is a fading argument. At some
point there won't be any more boxes of Jyhad left and then what? I'm
not touching them, in any case, because I don't want the mixed card
backs and lack of colour-coding. I can do without the hassle of
sorting and filing thousands of cards too. Those cards are obsolete
and your emphasis should now be on encouraging players to buy new WW
stock, not old, remaindered WotC stock. They will have to pay full
retail for the WW cards and this isn't going to be cheap even if you
only collect one of each rare. If there's no ceiling to the number of
each card required then the game can clearly become a money-pit and
this issue is certainly enough to stop me taking the game seriously.
If you want to get new players to try the game, you need to have an
answer to this objection. Telling them to read the archives ain't it.

If the PTB had any sense, they'd have multiple tournmant formats to
please both camps. Doomtown has four recognised formats: Bicycle (one
of each value), Derringer (CL=1), Double-Barrel (CL=2) and Standard
(CL=4). The standard format is the most popular but TOs can use the
other formats without all this unnecessary vituperation. What's wrong
with having a choice?

Andrew

Because it would be fracturing the player base to support a game that is not
the one desgined to be VTES. VTES was designed specifically to be a NCL game.

It already lies that way, if you are assuming you need 50+ of some
cards. Ben Peal's 60-Weather Control deck was a silly lark, and i
doubt even HE expected it to do anything other than gain a few VPs and
keep himself amused. Sure, he intended to TRY to win as much as he
could, but 60 of one card is the formula for NO winning deck.

You can easily compete seriously with a simple commons-only deck. The
solution lies in experience, and increased deck-building skill. Your
options may be slightly more limited because you have fewer cards, but
this is true whether or not you play under a CL.

If you don't have all the commons you want, I am CERTAIN that some can
be found for you in the UK. We have an enormous box here in Atlanta
that we call the "common/uncommon giveaway pile" that basically
consists of everyone's commons and uncommons that they have 40 of and
will never need more than 15 of - and that's assuming they keep
several decks built that use the card. When new players come into our
group, we point them at THAT box first, so they can be sure to have
plenty of the basic stuff for their decks, and that way they can be
basically competitive.

>other bigots tell me that no-one plays Star Wars, B5, Shadowfist,
>whatever. I don't even bother to cite VTES as few of them will have

Pokemon. "No-one", by comparison, plays any other CCG. What names
you get will depend on where you turn and who you ask, but those are
the two biggies.

>CL, it's about the storyline restricted format. VTES hasn't got there
>yet but I dare say it will. The equivalent issue will be banning
>Jyhad cards when the VTES base set is reprinted. That'll be fun...

And will never happen. There are rules right now to deal with
Jyhad-backed cards. They work fine. White Wolf is fully aware of the
original screwup that WotC made by changing the name of the game, and
they aren't about to compound the mistake by alienating all the
players with Jyhad cards, who are currently the people who are keeping
the game ALIVE.

>The starting point here is that the player base is already split. Why
>won't VEKN embrace the CL play-groups and recognise their way of
>playing the game?

Because it's wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, and wrong, and doesn't
serve any actual purpose. The game was designed for NCL. The player
base is not split, as the vast majority of players still use NCL. New
players will be introduced to the game as an NCL game, and will learn
it properly. So it won't be a problem.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <vovdrsggj6tpbppqa...@4ax.com>, Derek Ray
<lor...@yahoo.com> writes

>Let him get as many votes as he wants - intercept the ones which are
>actually a threat.

Your best option is to kill the Legacies, in my view. They *are* the
votes which are actually a threat.

The times I've seen LoP defeated, it's generally been when the deck has
been stalled very quickly. It couldn't do the vote in its first (i.e.
the second, normally) turn, so it had to wait for the third turn. By,
then, someone has normally been able to bring out a 7 or an 8 -
hopefully a voting vampire.

It's been a long standing habit of mine, when building crypts, to favour
having a couple of Princes, Justicars, Bishops (alter to taste) in the
crypt, simply for this ability. If I can get a Prince out - let's say
Rake, Rob has problems. He can get the edge, yes. He gets one vote
from the card, yes. Now he *needs* a vote push card (Awe, BewOra). And
if I'm not the only person doing this - the Gangrel player has just
brought out Caitlin, or Gitane, say - everyone stands a chance to vote
him down.

So why pick the Legacy of Pander? Well, it's quite common to have a
vote deck on a table or, at least, a deck that has the capacity to vote
in it, possibly as an aside, with a few cards around. Legacy of Pander
doesn't just work on their votes, it works on everyone's. You hand the
control of the entire voting environment to the LoP player. If you
block the Kine Resources Contested, he's still probably got a few more
votes up his sleeve, and he can still vote down your votes. If you
block the Legacy of Pander (either through intercept, Direct
Intervention, Delaying Tactics), then he can't kill your votes, and he
can't pass the Kine Resources Contested anyway.

> vampires...but surely that isn't broken, is it?) are "fun" and who
defines
> "fun"? And if they're not fun, why are they broken and thus
prohibited by
> your CL?

Sorry I missed to address your question, but here's the answer:

I agree these strategies seem fun to try out and I also agree that with
CL they're not really possible to try out to its fulle xtent. So that's
a negative yes, however on the positive side you get rid of some
potentially very powerful combos and that straight out very boring to
be faced it. It's not like there's absolutely no counter against these
strategies (like LoP, 15 deflect deck etc) but it's that they're just
really boring to face! We want some variety and not be the game
like "vote+BO, vote+BO, vote+BO" etc, see my point?

And as for the Raptor combo, nobody here owns more than 1 Raptor....I
used to have 3 but traded two away, so naturally nobody would come up
with the idea of suggesting we lifted CL coz they wante dot try this
combo. If it happened, I guess we'd have to make a discussion as to
whether we want to continue with the CL or not. It's really that
simple, as long as everybody is happy, we don't change it and people
won't question it since they're that, happy about it!

If I played with you guys using NCL I'd have to adapt and I don't think
I would have much of problems with it. But I do believe CL makes the
game more diversified, makes it last longer, and sums up to making ti
more fun in general.

I think that the *game lasts longer* argument is important too (at
least to me). The impression I get form you guys, is that if you have a
round wasted, or didn't get the combo you built your deck on in the
first few rounds, you're screwed. And it also sounds like ousting
someone after a few rounds isn't uncommon.

Well this isn't just how we want the game to be. I like games that are
a real sweat and very even, and where you can play for up to 4 hours
before it's settled. This doesn't mean our games cannot be quick
either, but at least it's normal that they last for 1,5-2 hours with 4
players. I'm pretty sure yours doesn't (normally).

specific

couldn't play a

to sweep
> the table time and again, but since I am entertained with odd deck
concepts, I
> would want to try it out.
>

> You may have noticed that I have continued to post on this thread.
Sorry, I'm

> Xian

>>Let him get as many votes as he wants - intercept the ones which are
>>actually a threat.
>
>Your best option is to kill the Legacies, in my view. They *are* the
>votes which are actually a threat.

Hm. Maybe this is just me, since when I play intercept, I tend to
build decks that can stop "any action, anywhere, any stealth".
(Superior Night Moves is excluded from this list.) So I tend to look
at it as idle entertainment until he actually tries to DO something
with his votes, at which point i offer him the deal "No damage to me,
or that vampire goes kaboom." Usually his vampire gets to go kaboom
at that point, although some of my decks (Daffy Deck, leggy? =) don't
make kaboom very well.

This is assuming he's my predator. If he's my prey, I seize every
opportunity to disrupt the hell out of his deck by stopping his
actions and punching his minions for 1, if necessary. =)

>The times I've seen LoP defeated, it's generally been when the deck has
>been stalled very quickly. It couldn't do the vote in its first (i.e.
>the second, normally) turn, so it had to wait for the third turn. By,
>then, someone has normally been able to bring out a 7 or an 8 -
>hopefully a voting vampire.

This is also an effective way to stomp it, or when someone else has
had a convenient KRCG, or Delaying Tactics, or Edge, or whatever.

>So why pick the Legacy of Pander? Well, it's quite common to have a
>vote deck on a table or, at least, a deck that has the capacity to vote
>in it, possibly as an aside, with a few cards around. Legacy of Pander
>doesn't just work on their votes, it works on everyone's. You hand the
>control of the entire voting environment to the LoP player. If you
>block the Kine Resources Contested, he's still probably got a few more
>votes up his sleeve, and he can still vote down your votes. If you
>block the Legacy of Pander (either through intercept, Direct
>Intervention, Delaying Tactics), then he can't kill your votes, and he
>can't pass the Kine Resources Contested anyway.

OK, I think I see the other half of it. I assume that my deck is NOT
necessarily going to have a vampire -and- intercept handy to stop the
first LoP, so he'll already have one vote per vampire - which could be
enough to pass stuff anyway. Certainly, from the point of view of a
voting deck, I would want to make sure he couldn't gain vote lock and
stomp my guys flat. But this is also something the table should
discuss IMMEDIATELY as soon as the first LoP hits the table - "Do we
need to make this deck dead NOW, or can we just stall it for a few
turns and let it die on its own?" I don't see LoP included as part of
many decks OTHER than the LoP deck, so it's usually safe to assume
that someone calling an LoP is about to attempt to run over the table.

There's always the potential option, in your own vote deck, of just
burning the early single LoP's as they come out. A Prince with
superior BO has 6 votes, which beats 5 Panders. (A Prince with Closed
Session can snub the Pander completely, and Closed Session isn't
always such a bad card.) And after that, he may have a difficult time
getting the next few LoP's out, since there probably won't be THAT
many vote modifiers of his own in the deck, and everyone else will
have had time to get some intercept ready, etc.

Whispers from the Dead is a +1 stealth action. Spectral Divination
and Giuseppe, Gravedigger make it +3 stealth, out of reach of any
single card *and* most importantly out of reach of 2nd tradition.
Seduction is nastier than you think since that guy you left untapped
just for that reason will suddenly be unable to block - you'll be
spending a lot of time attempting to block the card-fetch actions.

Carlotta's action is also at +1 stealth, and she has Obfuscate. (And
in this deck I would play with OBF skill masters and OBF stealth added
in, because there are a couple other Giovanni with Obfuscate as well.)

It may not be unblockable, but it WILL consistently gain more stealth
than you have intercept available.

The question is now, how do you abuse 4 Whispers from the Dead, the
Giovanni, and Carlotta? Oh look! Dominate bleed! =)

YEEE HAAAAAAA!

On a different note, it REALLY seems to me, from some things you say,
that you guys spend a lot of time habitually blocking. Is that true?
Often the best defense and/or strategy is to just not block someone.

to amputate a limb. It's part of MY game, and yes that's a reality.

The old "It's right because we say so" argument. Hmm.... convincing.

4CL was grafted onto Magic, and grafted badly. It didn't stop things
being broken, it didn't stop boring decks. Just look at the Magic scene
now - most of the time, it's half a dozen boring decks. 4CL didn't work
with Magic when it was started, so they invented restricted cards too.
All it did was force the "killer combos" into the "lucky" category. It
didn't make things more creative, because all you did was play lots of
different cards revolving around the same thing, rather than just the
one. Woohoo, you get killed by a Fireball instead of a Lightning Bolt.
Woohoo! And indeed, woohoo.

Magic has now been designed *with* a 4CL in mind - as have a number (the
majority) of other card games, though with subtle variations (3CL, 1CL
per character etc.) The card games are *designed* for it.

Jyhad was *not* designed for a card limit. This is reality. It was
specifically designed to be played with a theoretically infinite supply
of cards. Why do you think they went to so much trouble with things
like "1 named action modifier per minion per action", "1 source of
additional strikes per round", "1 named reaction per minion per action",
"1 master phase action per turn", "You may not cancel a maneuver you
played yourself", "You may not cancel a press you played yourself".

They tried to limit political actions, too, by limiting how many cards
you could replace. Play-testing didn't get that one right - but the
idea was there, and the intent was there, it just needed some tweaking.
The only real thing they didn't catch was actions - again, because play-
testing cannot catch everything, because you are not playing with every
person out there. The creative ideas *I* come up with are not the
creative ideas *you* come up with are not the creative ideas *Legbiter*
comes up with etc. Unless play-testing included every player who ever
has or will play V:TES on the planet, you couldn't predict everything.

So, for the most part, V:TES worked. The Gangrel infinite loop deck was
a trifle annoying, but was fixed with NRA, as was the Presence Bleed-
Block-Majesty-Wash-Rinse-Repeat deck. Two broken decks, and that was
it, basically.

A lot of people *perceived* Malkavian Stealth and Bleed as broken. It
was, indeed, a powerful deck - and still is. It could burn your pool
quickly and do it at stealth. There are, however, many counters to it.
Wake, Deflection is a good one. In a 4CL environment, that's 4 of each
I'm allowed. But you can take lots of bleed actions. I can bounce 4.
Woohoo and, again, woohoo. I can't have a good chance of drawing one in
my opening hand, with only 4 in the deck. I can't have a good chance of
having a steady flow of either, with only 4 in the deck. So, it's luck.
Does he bleed me when I have one, or not? Does he do his really big
bleed when I have one, or not?

If I wanted luck, I'd go play Battletech and roll lots of dice, instead
of relying on some skill in play and construction.

Works under a 4CL, you know. And it's an astoundingly competitive NL
deck.

Just because you are playing NL doesn't mean that *you* have to play a
deck with more than 4 of anything in. You can play whatever deck you
want and, once you have a reasonable pool of cards, you can build a
competitive set of decks. Something like a box of Jyhad is plenty to
make a very competitive deck. A box of V:TES or a box of Sabbat (though
finding the latter is nigh on impossible now) would do exactly the same,
since they give you, very roughly, a similar pool of cards. Legbiter
has done some astounding things with a box of Jyhad and a copy of the
"Happy Families" formula (.EXE version almost finished, I just need to
fix on error on one of the vampires), things you wouldn't believe. Some
of those fit in the 4CL category, others don't.

The idea that you have to have hundreds of rares to play NL is wrong,
based on assumption and mis-information.

Jyhad is *not* a game like Magic, where, from the off, some of the very,
very powerful cards were made stupidly more powerful than the commons.
That was never viewed to be likely as a problem, in Magic - since no-one
would have more than a couple, because there collection would never
exceed the heady heights of about 400. V:TES learned from this
fundamental error, so let's take a look at a couple of the instances
within Jyhad.

Misdirection: X pool - Tap X vampires. - Common
Anarch Troublemaker: Free - Tap 2 vampires *OR* burn equipment. - Rare

Yikes!

That's a fairly hefty difference. Misdirection has to pay 2 pool for
something Anarch Troublemaker gets for free *AND Anarch Troublemaker has
another ability. Clearly, the rares are more powerful than the
uncommons. Except, no - Anarch Troublemaker has some significant
downsides.

First of all, it isn't instant. You tap it during the untap phase, so
you have to go around a turn. Everyone has warning of it. Then, it
stays in play going to other people. It can come back and haunt you.
Then, it doesn't have the flexibility that Misdirection has. You can't
tap 5 vampires with Anarch Troublemaker, which you could do with
Misdirection.

The common card can be a lot more 'powerful' than the rare version, in
the right situation.

Then, we take Govern the Unaligned vs. Dominate Kine. Govern the
Unaligned is only 1 blood, and gets you +2 bleed, whereas Dominate Kine
is 2 blood, but only gets you +1 bleed *but* it also gives you +1
stealth. Swings and roundabouts. Then at superior, Govern the
Unaligned generates 3 pool for you, whereas Dominate Kine lets you steal
a location - useless, if there's nothing on the board. Swing and
roundabouts. The Rare version isn't more powerful, it's just a
different card.

Then take Fists of Death vs Undead Strength. First of all, Undead
Strength is free - but it's only for one strike. If you were to be
using it defensively (i.e. to deter people from rushing you), you
probably wouldn't have additional strikes, so Undead Strength would be
much better. If, however, you want to go offensively, play Fists of
Death as being better.

What about Undead Strength vs Torn Signpost? Well, again, you have to
pre-declare your intentions with Torn Signpost. There are no hidden
surprises, you can't just throw it on someone once they've said "strike
for hands", they know even before they set range. Then Undead Strength
complements it quite well, adding to the strike - so you could be
striking for 5. Also, the different periods in combat at which you play
them give you different opportunities. I could be drawing Undead
Strength after playing a few maneuver cards, for instance.

Similarly, versus Death of my Conscience, you can get, wow, +8 hand
damage from one card! But you have to discard cards, which is something
Undead Strength never makes you do. And it has a hefty blood cost, too.

Would a deck playing with Torn Signpost be, necessarily, better than one
with Undead Strength? No. It might be a slightly different deck, but
both of them could stand up to competitive play, albeit differently.

Rare cards *aren't* a way to win a game. A good deck is, and a good
deck doesn't require 20 of any card, nor rare cards at all.

That's a reality, and yes, it's that simple.

first round. It was the Black Lotus-Channel-Fireball deck. I don't
know if you have heard of it so I will tell you about it. On round one
A player would play a Black Lotus (which costs zero mana and the player
could tap it and discard it for 3 mana of any color), and a mountain.

burn 19 life, so he would have 2 red mana (one from the lotus and one
from the mountain) and 19 colourless mana. The player could then cast a
20 point fireball and take the opposing player out on round one.

or even the second round. The game was designed that way. Since there

Sometimes large multiples of cards are effective and sometimes they're
not. I'll leave interesting up to each individual person. You were
responding to a post by a UK player, and their environment (from what I
gather) has fewer _really_ focused decks than what you might find in the
US. I have a deck with 13 Immortal Grapples. I have a deck with 8
Earth Melds. Neither of these decks would function correctly under a
card limit. So having large (i.e. >= 5) multiples of cards is
effective, given that allowing such multiples allows particular decks to
exist and denying such disallows that existence.

To address the collection difficulty: I would say that I have a
reasonably large number of cards, but there's no way I could build 30
V:TES decks. I have a reasonably large number of Shadowfist cards, but
if I tried to make 30 decks, the last ten to fifteen or so would be
stuffed full of Lily Ponds or some such crap. The issue is whether it
is inordinately difficult to make _some_ deck under NCL. I would say
that the answer is "no", since there are a large number of decks that
can run on mostly commons and still be effective. Are there decks that
require a large number of rares to build? Yes. Can these decks be
beaten by the aforementioned "commons decks"? Also, yes. My Brujah
rush deck is chock full of rares and still stops dead in its tracks
against Skin of Steel, Obedience, or lots of maneuvers, none of which
are rare.

> Get a clue - it obviously keeps coming up because it's an important
> issue. It won't go away until it is resolved in a better way than
> ranting "wrong, wrong, wrong".

OK. I agree that it is an important issue. As the only card game
without an official card limit (as far as I am aware), V:TES has a
unique place in the CCG world. People are correct to ask: can this game
really work without a card limit? Even "cantila" agrees that the NCL
game is at least functional; he/she just doesn't like it. As people who
have been on this newsgroup for years and have had this discussion
repeatedly, we know why a lot of people are (for lack of a better word)
"afraid" of playing with NCL. "Cantila" is afraid that NCL makes for

(a) overly powerful decks,
(b) less interesting decks, and
(c) less fun overall.

We can only assure him/her that

(a) while NCL decks are generally more consistent, NCL tournaments are
_not_ dominated by one or two deck types,
(b) many people would argue that since many interesting decks are
impossible under CL (IG rush, Cryptic Missons, some Gangrel and Tremere
decks), NCL provides for more interesting decks overall, and
"consistent" does not equal "boring", and
(c) we are having just as much fun as you are.

I will close by mentioning again that I used to play 4CL, then switched
and was glad I did. So I _do_ understand the arguments.

To "cantila" I would only suggest that you misunderstand a lot about the
NCL environment. Few decks have 20+ of any cards. Decks with that
many, say, Majesties sound good on paper, but in practice they don't
really work. You have said that you don't put a limit on Corruptions
because of its unique effect. Would you be willing to raise the limit
on other cards which have such a unique effect, like Immortal Grapple,
Mind Numb, Aire of Elation, Cryptic Mission, Walk of Flame, etc.? If
not, why not?

James

than 1. That will end up hurting me when I don't get a Rush action in

>and blow their heads off since I haven't ended combat.
>> But if I'm fighting, say, the Assamites, I can use the superior and
>> end combat.
>
>If it was S:CE you included Staredown for you'd do better with Majesty
>where you get S:CE even at inferior.

This is why you need some more experience building decks, something
that NCL would provide you. You are totally missing the point.

If I include Majesty, I do not get the "dodge" feature. If I include
Sideslip, I do not get the S:CE feature. Using those specific cards
mean that I have to include twice as many cards in my deck just to
have a way to save my guys if I run into a bigger, meaner combat deck.
If I use Staredown, I can include, say, 8 of them in the deck, and I
have EITHER 8 Dodges *or* 8 S:CE cards, depending on what I need at
the time. If I just need to dodge someone's initial strike, then I
can do that and use the gun to shoot them for 4 afterwards. If I need
to get out of combat ENTIRELY, I can use the SAME CARD and do so.
This means instead of 16 cards (8 Majesty and 8 Sideslip), I can put
in only 8, which means that I will be more likely to draw cards like
.44, Blur, Legal Manipulation, Blood Doll, what have you, and have
them in my hand. This will make my combat more effective, since I
will have the cards I need when I need them.

In NCL, there is an opportunity cost for every card you put in your
deck. If you put a card in that is unnecessary, you will have to
discard that card. If I play a deck with 8 Majesty and 8 Sideslip,
then I will most likely not need BOTH the Majesty and the Sideslip in
the same game. I will end up discarding a bunch of one or the other,
and my deck will run poorly. If I play a deck with Staredown, I will
probably not ever have to discard one, and I can discard other cards
that I might not need instead.

> Staredown is a multiple-use card, and more flexible than
>> Majesty. In fact, thinking about it, I currently wish I had MORE
>> Staredown now, because it'd be entertaining to build a deck like that.
>
>Oh why don't I believe you?

Because you aren't thinking about it all the way through, and because
you don't have enough experience with NCL to understand the concept of
"opportunity cost"? In CL, there is little to no opportunity cost -
you stick in 4 of every cool card, and you never discard even if your
hand looks like shit, because you know you have to use every card. In
NCL, it requires much more skill to know where the fine line is.

This, by the way, is how you prepare for the unknown. First, ask
yourself what your deck will do: "OK, I have a Toreador/Brujah gun
deck. It will bleed with Presence, and fight with .44 Magnums and
Celerity Blurs if someone blocks it. It will have blood gain via
multiple Blood Dolls, and its vampires won't be spending much blood or
taking much damage in combat, so a lot can be pulled off them. Its
defense against basic bleed will be either leaving a gun untapped, or
Wake-and-block with a couple intercept locations, maybe some transient
Auspex cards since a lot of PRE/CEL guys are Toreador and have at
least inferior AUS. Its defense against voting or stealth bleed will
be its Rush actions, which can be taken backwards as necessary to
remove threats. Its defense against combat... hmm. How can I defend
against multiple combat types?"

Well, you have maneuvers from the guns and Celerity, so you probably
don't have to worry about Immortal Grapple decks too much, or indeed
any close-range-only deck. What kind of long-range decks would give
you trouble? The Assamites use long-range attacks, and they have
additional strikes. To survive this, you'll have to use S:CE.
Potence weenies will throw a Sewer Lid at you, but you only need to
Dodge that, and then you can shoot back. Gangrel could use Body Flare
or Song in the Dark, but again, you only need to Dodge that. Tremere
will be using Theft of Vitae: a simple dodge is satisfactory. Other
Celerity decks, either guns or a Potence pitch deck, will be using
addtional strikes: you need S:CE. Your biggest problem will be
someone using Drawing Out the Beast since it ruins your guns and
maneuvers all in one. But even here, you can Dodge a Gangrel's claws
and then use your Blur and +1 hand damage from DotB to punch him for
4. If he is using Scorpion Sting, you can S:CE instead.

Turns out that to feel confident that you can survive other players'
combat, you need both Dodge and S:CE. You could include Majesty and
Sideslip, and either risk having the wrong one when you need it most,
or having too many of both. Or you could include Staredown, which
provides you both options in one card slot, and a few Presence skill
cards for the guys who only have pre/CEL. That would work pretty
well.

This would be a good "first incarnation" of such a deck:

Thanks to ELDB again for making it possible to whip this up real quick
to prove a point.

So tell me, is this deck broken or boring? It violates your 4CL in 8
different places. But it also makes use of a card that you previously
didn't consider very useful at all, and it makes use of one in a way
you obviously hadn't thought of before. (and possibly that nobody

thread).

How many rares does it have, I wonder? Hmm. Well, it has 6 Psyche,

necessary since your vamps won't be losing much blood. Damn, this
looks like a deck full of commons and uncommons to me... and it also

trouble equipping the guns. Even only one gun wouldn't be bad. It
also looks a bit light on intercept, but one deck can't do everything.
Might be worth it to rip out the Taste of Vitae and use 4 Sport Bikes
instead.

Messages.Author: John Whelan

I just want to add my two cents regarding Cantila's belief that playing CL
encourages diversity in playing clans, and that NCL encourages people to
specialize in one clan.

I don't know if this is true, but if it is, then I think the "moral of the
story" is not what he thinks it is.

I am one of those NCL players he is talking about. I am well known
locally for being a Nosferatu specialist. Hell, I'm even a Camarilla
Nosferatu specialist -- my minions don't mix with those Sabbat scum! I
typically have 3 or 4 distinctly different Nosferatu decks prepared at any
given time, plus several dismantled designs that were good enough to
record for future use. I have a deep-stealth bleed deck that uses the
under-rated night-moves/spying-mission combo; a Lucretia deck; a Sheldon
intercept & Destroy deck (he kicks ass!); a baby-factory political deck; a
"bring out the clan" deck who's rather silly goal is to get all 23 vamps
on the table; a "Power of the Camarilla" ventrue/nos deck (which will
probably work better after Sabbat War is released); a basic nossie "rush"
deck; not to mention several discarded designs. I'd have more, except
that it can be exhausting to keep taking the decks apart again ... but I'm
certainly not at a loss for ideas. I occasionally play other clans, with
mixed success ... but there certainly seems to be more than enough
possibilities to explore in the Nossies to keep me busy for life.

All in all, I would say I play Nossies about 50% of the time. I might do
so more often if limited supply of Nossie cards did not prevent me from
having an unlimited quantity of different nossie decks prepared
simulaneously, or if I did not worry that my playgroup might learn to
exploit.

Nobody complains that I am being boring when I play Nossies, because most
of my decks are startlingly different from each other. Being subtly
undermined by Aggrippina at +6 stealth is very different from having
Sheldon rip your head off every time you dare take an action, which in
turn is very different from a horde of weenie nossie princes who can vote
themselves huge gobs of pool, and like to pull out disguised assault
rifles when attacked.

However, Cantila is probably right. Under 4CL, my creative options within
the Nossie clan would probably be far more limited, and I would be forced
to explore more clans more often in order to add sufficient variety to my
decks and keep myself and other players from getting bored. I don't see
this as a good thing, and I don't see how he could possibly see it that
way either. More creative options = good. Less = bad.

vamps anyway, and disciplines at superior, then a choice of effects can be
much more valuable than one single effect that is somewhat more powerful.

trade for, since no-one else thinks it's any good). Yeah, sure, the

get to choose what you need, and that's important.

those you block, but want to avoid getting too damaged yourself. Perhaps
the plan is simply to dodge, while a ghoul retainer blasts with
a flamethrower, or to dodge, and then additional strike. But before you
have to choose, you find that the blockee has played all kinds of nasty
effects and topped it off with a killer strike. Good thing this dodge
doubles as a S:CE!!!

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 8 Sep 2000, Andrew S. Davidson wrote:

> Better yet to do something about this when planning the pack-out for
> the new sets. It should be a golden rule in any CCG that the rares
> should be unique and the uniques should be rare. This has not been
> the case in VTES where there are many common vampires and unique
> master cards which are just waste paper. These should have been cards
> like Taste of Vitae.

I'm not sure you fully appreciate how well thought out the rarity system
is. While they may have made a goof on a card here or there, the Jyhad
designers put alot more thought into this than you seem to have.

Uniqueness is indeed one of the factors that is used to determine rarity.
There is only one common Unique card, and that is The Barrens -- a card
ideally suited for making beginning decks more playable. All other
uniques are uncommons, rares, or double-frequency rares (no
double-frequency uncommons).

Another factor used to determine rarity is clan-specific requirements (or
other requirement). Clearly, cards that are only usable by one specific
clan will not see play as often, or in as many decks, as a card that any
clan can use. So it makes sense that they be more rare. Again, we see
that this is the case: There are no common clan-specific cards ... all
are either uncommon or rare. Among cards that are both unique AND
clan-specific, all are either rares or double-frequency rares. The only
exceptions to this are the Hunting Grounds Cards, and, I think, one other
Uncommon per clan, which once again were seen as cards that beginning
players would find useful. (HG's are also not *as* clan specific as many
other cards, as once it is in play, any vamp can use it -- even if a
beginning player has only 3 or 4 Nossies in his crypt, a HG card is still
likely to be useful.) With a few exceptions, we see this principle
applied throught the set: political cards that require a prince or
justicar tend to be less common than ones that anyone can call, for
instance.

Another principle, which is kind of similar, is that cards that only work
well as part of combos do not need to be as common as cards that work well
on their own. Clearly, if card A works great by itself, but Card B only
works well in combination with card A, then you do not need to have as
many B's as you do A's. Some decks will have A by itself, and even a deck
that uses them in combination, if it is well designed, will have somewhat
more A's than B's. Perfect example is would be Undead Strengh as opposed
to Growing Fury. Thrown Gate is a common, since it can be used to
good effect in any combat. Well-Aimed Car, however, can only be used from
long range on the second round of combat (requiring both a press and a
manuever). Therefore it is uncommon. Example 2: Torn Signpost is
Uncommon, and can be used to good effect in any combat. Fists of Death is
clearly worse than Torn Signpost, because it costs a blood. Its advantage
is that it is cumulative. Thus, it does not make sense to play Fists of
Death unless you play Torn Signpost first. It makes perfect sense, then,
for Fists of Death to be rarer than Torn Signpost (though in this case
they ought to have been more common than they are, since they are clearly
more usable than, say, Growing Fury or Well-Aimed Car; part of the
problem is that they became more useful than originally intended due to
the V:tES rules changes; another part is that press combat did not
assume the importance intended for it due to its inability to compete
with S:CE, and second-round specialty cards like Growing Fury thereby
became wallpaper).

I'm not sure what your point is regarding "common vampires". All
vampires, of course, are equally common (approximately the same frequency
as an "Uncommon"), and if you have an unusual sized heap of some vampire
you regard as particularly useless, that is simply a result of random
luck. Vampires, of course, are the very basis of play in Jyhad, and the
designers needed to ensure that the beginning player would have enough of
them to get started. The inevitable result is that players with large
collections end up with a few too many of each. The situation, however,
is a big improvement over that of Land Cards, which serve as the basis of
play in M:tG -- you don't see Vampire player throwing out crypt cards by
the truckload.

The problem with Taste of Vitae is merely that it turned out to be far
more useful and in demand than the game designers anticipated or intended.
The designers probably thought of it as a disciplineless, inferior variant
of a Tremere's "steal blood" effects, when actually it can be far more
effective, because, unlike the latter, it can be combined with damage
dealing strikes. In the minds of designers it was probably intended to be
no more useful than Amaranth (also a disciplineless, uncommon, combat
card). And how many folks complain that they don't have enough of them?

-- John Whelan

instance, that the vampires in my crypt have mostly "cel PRE" (Mariana
Gilbert being the youngest example).

because unlike ANY of those dodges it also offers a choice of
S:CE. Mariana cannot use the superior version of celerity dodge cards,
because she does not have superior celerity. None of those dodges will be

pre. However, even a combat deck might want PRE if it also relies on
voting. Depends on the deck you are making.

combat, if that is what my strategy is. However, if I have a Ghoul
Retainer and a Flamethrower, I might prefer to dodge -- with an S:CE as a

but can we get too specific in this kind of argument? Surely your
argument depends on showing that Staredown is a much worse card in a far
more general sense -- to the point where it is a much better choice than
majesty in almost all situations.

> On Sat, 9 Sep 2000 03:23:40 -0400, John Whelan wrote:

My discussion was concerning the original set (Jyhad/Vampire) which, so
far as I could tell, was what was being complained about. I'm also
familiar with the Sabbat set, and what I discussed applies there as
well. Indeed, the Sabbat set has so many clans and disciplines to service
that the game cannot function as a standalone set unless the designers
ensure that the common cards are the ones are widely usable, with
clan-specific cards and uniques always being less common. One of the
purposes of the rarity scheme is to ensure playability with a minimum
number of cards.

There were only 2 rarity levels in the Dark Sovreigns set, "Common" and
"Uncommon". Oxford U is a "Common", which is not consistent with the
Jyhad scheme. In Ancient Hearts they reintroduced 3 rarities again,
probably because "Uncommon" had not turned out to be rare enough in the DS
set, and people complained about getting too many of some things.

lists". (Double frequency cards say "Rare 2, 3" for instance, instead of
just "Rare 3").

No vampires were printed twice, but you're right... there is more to the
story. There were 120 slots on the vampire sheets. The remaining 9 were
filled by Political actions. The following are the 9, and their rarity is
typically listed as "Vampire" since they are just as rare as vampires.

Kindred Restructure
Kindred Segregation
Lextalionis
Masquerade Enforcement
Parity Shift
Praxis Solomon
Reversal of Fortunes
Dramatic Upheaval
Archon

If you ever open a new Jyhad starter or booster, check out the vampires.
Usually you will get (I think) 4 of them per booster. Occasionally, you
will get only 3, and one of the above cards will be mixed in among them.
That is because the rule is not 4 vampires, but rather 4 cards from the
"vampire sheet". If you check your supplies of these cards, you will
likely find you have between 3 and 9 of them, just like with your
vampires.

I would guess that the odds of getting only one Lucia in a collection your
size are less than 1 in 100, but since you have more than 100 vampires, it
is no great surprise it happened to one of them.

-- John Whelan

On Sat, 9 Sep 2000 X_Ze...@email.msn.com wrote:

> Why shouldn't a solid Corruption-strategy be wallpapered just like a
> solid Cryptic Mission strategy. Corruption is far more powerful in game
> terms. So why can I play a deck that has 40 Corruptions in it and not
> on that has 40 Cryptic Missions. The Corruption deck is much
> scarier. BTW, I have seen decks posted that have that many Corruptions.
>
> I is not that the card is useless but rather that it hoses a whole
> strategy if you limit a card to 4 per deck.

Yes, but those are two different issues, so it is unfair to call him a
inconsistent if he makes an exception for one case, but not the other.

Bear in mind that I am not in favor of CL. I agree that it limits
creative options, including (but not limited to) decks based on cryptic
mission. Under CL, most of my decks would be disallowed. But Cantila
evidently feels that he gains something from such a rule that is worth the
sacrifice (and it is possible that he is right within the limited context
of his playgroup -- I have more thoughts on that which I shall post
later). That being his position, it would not make sense for him to start
making 1,000 exceptions for specific cards. House rules, like errata,
should be kept simple and to a minimum.

If you want to accuse him of inconsistency, I suspect he is far more
vulnerable on the issue of skill cards. These, clearly, will limit your
decks design options if you can only use 4 of them -- which is the precise
same issue as limiting cryptic missions. And skill cards are clearly not
in the same category as Corruption -- they clearly ARE useful, even if you
only play one of them.

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 10 Sep 2000 X_Ze...@email.msn.com wrote:

> Why is it the clear and obvious choice?

Depends on the criterion used to make exceptions. In this case, the
justification is that the *card* was clearly designed to be used without
limits, and becomes wallpaper if not used that way. Apply the same
criteria to any other *card*, and I don't think you can make as good a
case for it.

> if you limit it to 4 now you
> can only corrupt weenies. You must base your deck around something else
> (stealth-bleed, stealth politics, mind-numb). Tough turds. My point is
> if you are going to defend CL then at least play by CL; not, CL with the
> exception of Action Card A or Master Card B. That is hypocrisy by
> making exceptions for one or two cards or even worse one or two types of
> cards.
>
> Hypocrisy is the very symptom that he cannot defend.

I don't understand this focus on the "hypocrisy" issue. This is not
exactly a moral issue, and it's not like he fails to practice what he
preaches (however irrational you feel his justifications are).

Is it not possible that 4CL serves some kind of function within the
context of the low-supply card environment he plays in? Is it not a
simple rule that is easy to remember?

If so, might it not be equally true that 4CL, with 2 exceptions, may serve
the same purpose, and still be simple enough for everyone to remember?

But you say if he makes 2 exceptions, he should make 20 or 30 or 40,
because otherwise he is a "hypocrite". That makes no sense to me at
all. Even if it is conceded that his two exceptions are somewhat
arbitrary, his system is still better than this alternative, because a CL
rule with 30 or 40 exceptions is just to clumsy to be workable -- too
complex to be easily remembered.

A fourth option, of course, is to dispense with CL entirely, but that
overlooks that possibility that CL might serve some helpful purpose within
the context of his playgroup ... which is what he is claiming.

There are plenty of excellent arguments you can make against CL. This is
not one of them. All games have rules which have been defined on a
somewhat arbitrary basis. Calling someone a "hypocrite" because his House
Rules have arbitrary features makes no sense.

-- John Whelan

OK, I lied. Parts of this post are just too mind-numbingly stupid. I
absolutely MUST respond.

On Tue, 12 Sep 2000 02:09:50 GMT, cantila <rogc...@student.luth.se>
wrote:

>Because a basic defence against somehting won't be enough against a
>deck specialized in the same area.

WRONG. This is the core concept that you have failed to grasp.

- +1 intercept will abuse a Ventrue vote deck. This is basic.
- Nossie vote decks get around +1 intercept. Dread Gaze, Surprise
Influence, or titled vampires will slap that around.
- Setite vote decks will get around both. Setite vote decks take
forever to get started - a fast deck will beat them. Also, Setite
decks tend to be a bit light on combat defense because it takes so
many cards to make the deck go - a Rush deck will kill them.
- Fortitude/Obedience will stop a Rush deck, so play the Ventrue. See
how we've come in a big circle?

A basic defense will be sufficient against most of what you will face.

>If you have a a basic vote defence, you won't be able to stop a heavy
>vote-going Ventrue through your vote defence.

"basic vote defence: +1 intercept"

The most likely (and most lethal) voters are the Ventrue. If you want
to bet on the odds, include +1 intercept. If you KNOW Bob is playing
his Nosferatu Vote Machine with Forgotten Labyrinth, better change
your plan. But in general, +1 intercept and a few titled vamps will
put a wrench in a lot of vote decks. Delaying Tactics will screw
almost EVERY vote deck, but there's only so many you can put in your
own. If you haven't considered votes at all, you lose 100% of the
time. Better to give yourself a chance.

>And naturally, you can't have good defence in all areas. If youd id,
>then there would be no loopholes to exploit, which you yourself said
>always exists.

correct! See rock-paper-scissors example above.

>With NCL that means that I can make my deck very very strong in one
>area and have it suck in most tohers, but if you don't make a very very
>good defence in the area I'm so storng in, then I'll win over you in
>that area. And done good enough I'll have a deck that will almsot
>always win, until you make a deck that specifically counters mine. But
>that requires you to know my deck dude. And you're saying you don't
>need to.

And you are very, very wrong. Decks that almost always win are nearly
unheard of. The Legacy of Pander deck does not almost always win.
Todd Banister tried MANY times to make one go. We kept stepping on
it, partly because he had horrible luck drawing a LoP in his opening
hand. The TGP deck does not almost always win, and I saw Legbiter
play it NUMEROUS times - it took a LOT of skilled play on his part to
get the VPs he gained. It is not simply a case of "ok, my turn. I
tempt that vampire. I Parity Shift. Next." and then lather, rinse,
repeat! It is MUCH different.

You Do Not Need To Know Someone's Deck. This Is Fact.

Sometimes you will sit down next to a deck that just happens to be the
antithesis of yours - for example, you may be playing a nice weenie
bleed deck with no intercept and only Deflection, and the Ventrue Vote
Machine sits down behind you. You may die miserably. (Actually, even
then you have a chance to win by just outracing it.) These things
happen. You will adapt and live with it, or fail. You could begin
politicking to get help from the table. There are LOTS of things you
can do. You are far from helpless.

You refuse to believe this, but you have never played in an NCL
environment, and you do not have the deck-building skills or play
experience to understand how absolutely, completely true it is. You
are also too stubborn and mule-headed to admit it.

>If you've never faced a ToGP deck or heard of it, I find it quite
>unlikely that you'll win over it the first time you play. If you do,
>that's to the most part just luck (for example, you happeend to play a
>vote deck with lots of Wrath of Inner Circles ;)

If you've never heard of it, then the TGP player has the advantage of
surprise from a new concept, and surprise counts as "deck building
skill". If you HAVE heard of it, this still does not count as knowing
someone's deck, as there are several ways to play a TGP deck, and you
can't identify which they're using until they drop the TGP. Not to
mention that if you built your deck specifically to counter TGP, then
you will probably lose 3/4 of your games due to not sitting next to a
TGP deck.

(cantila's mythical Mind Numb strategy snipped)

It really amazes me how you can blather so endlessly about something
you obviously know nothing about. I refer you to...

Card text for Mind Numb:

(D) Put this card on any untapped vampire. Tap that vampire; he or she
does not untap during his or her controller's untap phase. Burn this
card at the beginning of your next untap phase. (S) As above, with +1
stealth.

Notice where it says UNTAPPED VAMPIRE? All this glop you're spouting
is totally pointless. Once you play one Mind Numb, I will never,
ever, ever, ever, ever leave a vampire untapped again, unless I am
packing intercept or have just transferred him out. Your 15 Mind
Numbs will pathetically clog your hand, and you will be discarding one
each turn while I laugh as you frantically search for bleed cards.

Second, zero stealth actions don't mean shit to an untapped vampire,
and +1 stealth actions aren't much more frightening. So what you need
to get +2 stealth on your Mind Numb is: A Marijava Ghoul (costs 2 and
a +1 stealth action to equip - and by the way, people go OUT OF THEIR
WAY to block Marijava Ghouls), and superior Presence. Not so easy,
now is it?

Third, James listed about 20 counters to your deck, any of which might
be in his. Since he doesn't know what you're playing, the odds are
about 1 in 20 that he'll have any specific counter. But he'll have
ONE, in some form or other.

However, YOU only have one deck. You do not have room for the 20
counters to his 20 decks. You have to pick and choose. So you use
Setites and OBF - that's great. You probably have no combat defense,
and you lack superior PRE. Maybe you include a bunch of PRE and
Marijava Ghouls - but you lose when he plays Rat's Warning on the
zero-stealth bleed action, and Cat's Guidance afterwards - his Numb
vampire is now untapped, and can take all the actions it wants.

Use your HEAD for a change. Yes, Mind Numb is a good card. Yes, it
can be very annoying. NO, it is not overpowered, because putting
10-15 in a deck would just screw yourself. Don't you think we'd hear
about all those nasty Mind Numb decks otherwise?

stealth with an equal amount of dedicated intercept is wrong. It
requires approximately twice as much dedicated intercept to catch a
dedicated stealth deck. The reason for this is Elder Impersonation. At
superior, Elder Impersonation causes a block to fail. This card single
handedly takes a vampire with alot of intercept on him out of the
blocking scheme and therefore requires the blocking player to put an
equal amount of intercept on a second vampire. Therefore it requires
twice as much intercept on average to catch stealth in any environment
CL or NCL. If you plan on playing Elder Impersonation, then it should
be your last of a series of stealth cards with your intention being to
draw out all of your prey's intercept.

Second, Malkavians can go all out every turn and bleed you with each
minion for two if you have Protected Resources, but if you have
protected resources then you cannot bleed your prey so therefore you
must play politics or you lose your Protected Resources. Therefore if
you play Protected Resources then you can't use a rush strategy, because

counter to Stealth/Bleed.

. He is either going to bleed you for no more than three or try to draw

definative defense against stealth and bleeds. It is convenient, cheap

"cantila" <rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote in message
news:8pk38v$ae$1...@nnrp1.deja.com...

> I have so damn many times. IG IG IG IG rings a bell? YOU haven't
> addressed how to deal with S:CE effectively with a common card.
>
> I wonder why you haven't??

Perhaps because there was no need to create a *common* counter to S:CE. As a
specialized case, an anti-S:CE card should be uncommon at best. Psyche is
uncommon. Fast Reactions is uncommon, as is Hidden Lurker. IG (as of Sabbat)
is uncommon, and arguably should have been uncommon in Jyhad/V:tES. Dog Pack
is Rare, and perhaps rightly so. It's a nice retainer. Sticks around for
quite a while. (All rarities are approximate...I don't really remember.)

You can deal with S:CE relatively effectively if you are packing more Haven
Uncovered and Bum's Rushes than the S:CE'er. However, this is a less elegant
solution and tends to waste more cards than other methods. If you could only
rely on these two cards, and no other effects to deal with S:CE, you would
probably need to pack approximately twice as many as currently tend to go into
a "killer" rush deck. Say 20 or so Bums' Rush and 8 Haven Uncovered. This
takes up a lot of deck space that could be devoted to other stuff. A few
cards providing an anti-S:CE effect aren't that scary because they are so
specific.

IG hoses S:CE, thaumaturgy and weapons for the first round only. Of these, in
the tournament scene at least, S:CE is the only one that sees much play.
Beyond that, all you get is a press and range-set for the next round. And
that's at superior. Not a lot for placing the card in your deck.

Psyche is a press at inferior, and at superior allows you to start a new
combat. Maybe worse than IG, but offers advantages in possibly making the
opponent blow 2 S:CE cards for your one card. Additionally, it has the
alternate use as a press if necessary. This card is perhaps more generally
useful than IG.

Fast Reactions is pretty much the same, except it disallows a strike by the
opposing minion on the first round and requires another ready untapped
vampire. Same with Hidden Lurker. Nice, but harder to implement than either
of our two previous choices.

Dog Pack, which a) costs a pool, b) takes an action to equip, and c) is pretty
darn fragile, is extremely useful for being placed in play until destroyed.
Nice. If only more clans had stuff like this. It's powerful.

Beyond that, as mentioned, BR & HU work, but only to a lesser extent. They
require too much space devoted to them alone to act as an effective counter to
S:CE.

Anyway, the whole point here is that a common should not necessarily have a
rarity that equates to its counter. S:CE is such a specific (and powerful)
effect that it need not have a counter that can be acquired in the same
quantities easily.

I've been up for 24 hours, so perhaps I'm not entirely lucid at this point.
Maybe someone else can translate for me.

This is simply wrong.

In NCL decks, everyone's offense fits into one of
three basic categories: vote, bleed, combat. If

defensive cards against vote, bleed, and combat.
You don't have to know exactly how your opponents
will be bleeding you, voting against you, or what
they'll be playing in combat to put in cards that
defend against their strategies. It's good to have
some idea of what the more popular approaches to
offense are, so that you pick the defensive cards
that will be most effective most often, but Delaying
Tactics works every time someone calls a vote, Obedience
works every time a younger vampire attempts to enter
combat with one of your DOM vamps, and Deflection works
every time someone tries to bleed you.

it's

This Mind Numb thing is totally misguided, as far as I
can see. Problem 1: You can only Mind Numb an untapped
vampire, by card text. (Which is why always tapping out
your vampires to take actions on your own turn is a total
Mind Numb defense and has the added benefit of clogging
the Mind Numb deck's hand with Mind Numbs.) Problem 2:
Taking two actions to get a bleed through is inefficient
and slow; three (with Marijava Ghouls) is even worse.
I've seen people try to make Mind Numb decks, and they
have never looked very powerful, because they simply cannot
be that fast.

[really big snip]

> No because commons can't always replace a rare. You showed plenty of
> strategies above against a MN deck that my group couldn't play against
> me if I made such a deck. And they'd not be able to do an MN deck
> themselves either unless they bought a lot of MN's. (I can't either,
> but I could spend money to buy them and they couldn't). There's heaps
> of other "cool" startegies they can't tyr out for this reaosn...and
> buying commons gets xpensive too when you need to buy a lot of them
> since there's so many different commons.

The rares in Jyhad are almost always *not* power cards.
They may be useful. They may be interesting. But they
are not the staple cards of the no-card-limit game. There
are about a zillion good bleed and vote cards that are
common, not to mention stealth, intercept, and combat.
The entire basis of the no-limits game is using a bunch
of common cards to make your deck work. That's why you
don't have to be rich to play no-limits Jyhad: You don't
need a heap of rares. You just need a heap of commons.

My interpretation of why your group likes card limits (and
I apologize if this is offensive) is that, first of all,
they don't like seeing the same card title a lot of times
in a game - they find it amusing to see different cards
used for the same effect instead. Second, nobody is
interested in "playing to win" - your players don't believe
that what's fun about the game is the competition for victory
points, but something else. Taking actions and having combats
and votes and such, maybe. But they're not interested in
putting together cutthroat decks and trying their best to
kill each other as effectively as they can, even by coming
up with clever and bizarre new deck concepts. Third, they
believe that if there were no card limits, the people with
more cards would automatically win by being able to put in
more copies of the "powerful" cards, and they are not
interested in buying enough cards (a couple boxes of Jyhad
each, maybe) to build the archetypal mostly-commons no-limits
decks.

Josh

Answer what?

That Elder Impersonation is a good argument for a card limit?

The following is a truism. Read it carefully.

A card that is unbalancing and detrimental to the game as whole is just
as unbalanced in a NCL environment as it is in a xCL environment. In
fact, in most cases it becomes even more unbalanced in xCL environments
as the ability to counteract the card also becomes more difficult.

The realitiy is that CL doesn't fix broken cards, it just makes them
played less frequently...and if I use Carlotta Giovanni (or Necromancy
cards) to go get the broken card out of my ash heap and back into my
hand, card limits become totally pointless and others will not be able
to reliably defend against it.

As for Elder Impersonation, while one vampire may not be able to block,
others can (and. like all action mods, only one Elder Intervention can
be played per action) so only players with one available blocker (and no
wakes) will be hurt by the card. If you're esp. worried about this card
(or any others), perhaps adding a few Direct Interventions to your decks
would be worthwhile.

Granted it's a rough card, esp. when coupled with Seduction, but it is
in no way is a good argument for card limits.

That said, card limits are _not_ part of the game (regardless of
whatever house rules you choose to invent) and the entire discussion of
card limits is pointless.

I think we are missing the point of the whole conversation, but I could be
wrong... I have been wrong before...(I think it was 1986)...;-)

This shouldn't be about CL vs. NCL. When the game was first designed, and
produced and the rule book came out, as I can recall correct me please if I
am incorrect, there was nothing stating card limits. I first played this
game with a CL, I played at a Magic:TCH store. That says it all. I did
however find out that the official rules of the game were to play with NCL,
and I said oh well, and adapted my decks accordingly. Sure I had traded
some cards away that I would have used in an NCL environment, but I got them
back realizing that I wasn't following the rules.

This CL that Cantila and friends have incorporated in their group (with
approval of the other coterie members) is an arbitrary decision that they
wish to follow. As long as they know they can't hold any sanctioned
tourneys with CL's in place (judging by the threads this won't happen
anytime soon) all should be well. They want to play this way, and it is
truly up to them whether or not to play with CL's or not.

This is where I get nasty... (sorry Cantila)...

When I found out the CL we had in our coterie was not part of the rules, we
banished it accordingly. Not playing by official rules is something I could
not comprehend. If I was playing Scrabble, can I decide that Double Word
Scores are actually Quadruple Word Scores? Would that make the game more
fair? More fun? Hard to say... but I wouldn't play a game without
following the rules to the letter. This is why alot of players feel that
CL's are bad. They just don't want to admit that they are being good boys
and following the rules. Playing with CL's in place is the equivalent of
breaking the rules. Like I said upfront... this shouldn't be about CL vs.
NCL... it should be about playing by official rules versus playing by your
own set of rules.

Just my opinion, and you know what an opinion is worth... NOTHING.

Preceding the Mark Langsdorf $150 reward, I had a reward offer up.

At the time, the current tournament rules were not in place, and I
drafted what would one day form the core of these rules (which are, as
an aside, No-Limit).

I challenged anyone to make a deck that was broken with the rules I had
proposed, and I offered a reward to do so. The reason: I wanted
people to either "put up or shut up". The old arguments about NL being
broken had been hashed over too many times, and I was tired of people

certain Mark feels the same.

abused the card quite ridiculously. Eventually, Return to Innocence
was banned.

the money, mostly because he felt guilty because it was the card that

in your hand, and keep cycling for more cards until you

-cards doesn't, instead they have like 10 Lasombra decks etc that they
-never break down. I think that tells something...

What does it tell? That it is a collectable card game, not Monopoly?
That the only way cards get printed is if people buy them?
That the only way stores have cards in stock is if people buy the
collectable card game? If people aren't buying cards, the game
is dead. We've been playing a dead game for 4 years. Lets
not kill it again with artificially deciding that money equals evil.
Or, that money equals boring. Or, that money equals winning.
It doesn't.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

-CL is an interesting challenge too, but as I can see you don't
-seem to be the courageous type wanting to try new and odd decks
-with some diversity :)

Does diversity in one single game in one single deck,
overpower the need for diversity in the game as a whole?

Take a set of all possible decks, subtract those that are prohibited
by a card limit. By definition, card limits reduce diversity in the
game.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

I played and advocated card limits from 1994 until 1996 when
the Sabbat came out. At that time, there was enough duplication
in the function of the common cards, that the ridiculousness of
a card limit became immediately obvious. I'm sorry you haven't
had the fortune to have players interested in the game when
it was available, because I never had problems buying the cards
in the areas I played until 1998, and then I still had no problem
finding the cards online.

Carpe Noctem.

cantila <rogc...@student.luth.se> writes:

>It's been stated in virtually all of my posts in this thread why CL for
>us is better than NL. A CL is good because the ones that do have the
>money to buy a lot of cards will then not be able to get too powerful.

>For example if someone needed X cards to defend against deck Y decently
>because deck Y has Z amount of card A that X is the best counter to,
>then with a limit, player with deck Y can only have 4 of card Y instead
>of 8. And if nobody or close ot nobody, can get a lot of card X, then

>this is a good thing. Else the player of deck Y could get more than 4

>of card A and it wouldn't be a good thing. This problem might not seem
>big, for one certain card, but then imagine it applies to all of the
>Sabbat and AH cards things are different.

The problem with analysis by conjectured example is that it ignores other
examples that seem to show the opposite. And it ignores which conjuctures
are likely to be more representive of the kind of stuff that happens in
reality.

The counter example to the above is when card limits help rather than
hinder players who have a lot of money become more powerful. For instance,
to run weeny political decks, you typically need some presense vote
modifiers to pass your first few votes to put titles on you weenies and
to overcome resistance in subsequenct votes that are close, for whatever
reason. Without card limits, this is typically done with Bewitching
Oration, a common-as-dirt Jyhad card. Put in card limits and you may not
be able to run the deck unless you can throw in multiple copies of a
several-bucks-a-pop Sabbat rare called "Awe". I've never played CL myself
but the defenders of NCL claim these examples are far more important than
the ones you're talking about. Since I've found very few rare, expensive
cards I'd violate any reasonable card limits on, I suspect they're probably
correct.

The problem you're concerned about seems better addressed by some kind of
point system that assigns points to how hard/expensive a card is to obtain.
Then put some kind of point limit on decks.

Fred

Messages.Author: Nystulc
Messages.Body:
Andrew S. Davidson wrote:

>My impression is that buying the expansions defocusses your collection
>rather than otherwise. If I buy more cards, my priority will be

>getting more VTES. Dark Sovereigns, Ancient Hearts, Sabbat (War) and
>the following set are all of little interest to me as they mostly
>develop other clans and these seem less interesting. Only after I'd
>bought enough VTES to get 10 or so power cards like Temptation of
>Greater Power, would I consider buying significant amounts of the
>other stuff.

Based on the above, it would seem to me that your impressions are clearly
misguided. Chasing rare cards from any collection is a very inefficient and
cost-intensive way of enhancing your strategic options and card choices,
expecially if you have other options available, like obtaining commons and
uncommons from other sets.

By the time you collect 10 of each rare from the V:tES set, very likely you
will have (unless you are buying rares individually) 40 of each uncommon and
140 of each common., as well as about 40 of each vampire.

Clearly you could have done better to make a much smaller investment in AH/DS,
Sabbat, and Sabbat War. This would have gotten you 8 extra vampires for your
favorite Camarilla clan, a large number of new cards for your favorite
disciplines, as well as a variety of other options. Vampires of new clans are
often valuable in deck strategies that are not based strongly on clan
affiliation. Tansu Bekir is a fine addition to a Nossie Obfuscate Deck, and
the Anti-Brujah work great in most Brujah Combat decks. Vampires are the very
basis of efficient deck design, and completing your collection of available
vampires from any set should probably take precedence towards chasing obscure
rares.

There are no "power rares" in V:tES. Those few that were inadvertently printed
have been errata'd. AFAIK, the "abusive" potential of Temptation of Greater
Power was discovered only recently, and it is a good bet that the game
designers themselves were unaware of it. Whether it needs to be errata'd is
doubtful, as you are probably giving too little credit to the skills of the
deck designer, and giving inadequate time for the metagame to adjust. Besides,
if you are really concerned about ToGP you might want to invest in DS/AH and
obtain a few copies of Fear of Mekhet and Wrath of the Inner Circle, which both
hose Justicars.

BTW, I am curious about the details of this abusive ToGP deck. Is it posted
anywhere?

-- John Whelan
